Abstract
The likelihood input to a Bayesian analysis almost never exactly represents how the
data were generated, calling into question the validity of posterior inferences. We review
a variational interpretation of the Bayesian posterior as an alternative justification
for its use under model misspecification, and consider the resulting implications on
uncertainty quantification and parameter estimation. We then introduce a range of
techniques that seek to obtain generalised Bayesian inferences that account for model
misspecification.
Keywords: Generalised Bayes; Gibbs posteriors; Robustness; Sensitivity analysis; Uncer-
tainty quantification
1 Introduction
In the Bayesian paradigm (see Bayesian Inference), inferences about parameters 𝜃 ∈ Θ ⊆
ℝ𝑝 from data 𝑦 = (𝑦 1, … , 𝑦𝑛) ∈ 𝒴 𝑛 are made using the posterior distribution (see Posterior
Distribution: Introduction ). The density of this posterior distribution is given by the
Bayes’ rule as
𝜋(𝜃 ∣ 𝑦) ∶= 𝜋(𝜃)𝑝(𝑦; 𝜃)
∫Θ 𝜋(𝜃)𝑝(𝑦; 𝜃)𝑑𝜃 , (1)
where 𝜋(𝜃) corresponds to the prior density for 𝜃, and 𝑝(𝑦; 𝜃) is the likelihood that data
𝑦 were observed under parameter 𝜃. The assumptions underlying inference through ( 1)
include that 𝜋(𝜃) exactly encodes the user’s beliefs about the plausibility of values of 𝜃
before the data 𝑦 were observed, and that 𝑝(𝑦; 𝜃) exactly correspond to how the data were

title: Analysis and Control of Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand Systems
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2106.14827v2
published: 2021-06-28T16:03:37Z
summary: Challenged by urbanization and increasing travel needs, existing transportation systems need new mobility paradigms. In this article, we present the emerging concept of autonomous mobility-on-demand, whereby centrally orchestrated fleets of autonomous vehicles provide mobility service to customers. We provide a comprehensive review of methods and tools to model and solve problems related to autonomous mobility-on-demand systems. Specifically, we first identify problem settings for their analysis and control, from both operational and planning perspectives. We then review modeling aspects, including transportation networks, transportation demand, congestion, operational constraints, and interactions with existing infrastructure. Thereafter, we provide a systematic analysis of existing solution methods and performance metrics, highlighting trends and trade-offs. Finally, we present various directions for further research.

Title:
AUDITA: certified auditing and causal attribution of adverse outcomes in autonomous multi-agent systems
Authors:
Zhixu Du
,
Yiran Chen
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract:
Physical automation is scaling toward fleets of embodied machines commanded by an AI brain. Early deployments already run factories and warehouses at production rates beyond any human line, and their adoption is accelerating. But when their joint decisions cause harm, everyone involved has reason to blame everyone else, the machine vendor, the algorithm provider, the factory operator, the insurer, and the regulator, and no method can divide the responsibility between them. Existing methods read logs whose origin they cannot verify and name a single culprit, misrepresenting outcomes that are overdetermined, preempted, or caused by an omission. We present AUDITA, an audit layer pairing a tamper-evident record of every inter-agent command with a certified, graded causal-attribution engine. We prove its verdict cannot be gamed: a rule-following agent can never be made to look guilty, an attempt to shift blame is itself caught and graded, and we establish the exact limit of what an evidence-based auditor can certify. On live language-model pipelines it reduces the standard judge baseline's responsibility error roughly threefold; on a benchmark of accident-grounded structures it recovers responsibility where single-culprit baselines fail, and stays invariant under forgery. AUDITA turns the question of who is to blame from an argument about logs into a calculation over evidence.

Abstract:
Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.
